content.text: So I've noticed a couple of issues with OAuth sessions with my malpercio.dev account. I can successfully log in to Tangled.org, and it appears to have kept sessions just fine over the timespan of days. I can get through the flow with rpg.actor, but when I land back at the app, I'm not actually logged in. And with pckt.blog, when I attempt to log in, I am met with "The client_id is not registered with this server" from pds.obsign.org. What's going on, why does our oauth behave differently with each?
I'll dig into the PDS OAuth implementation to figure out why three atproto clients behave three different ways. Let me start by finding the client-registration / client-metadata handling.

Confirmed — the constructor literally defaults `responseMode: r = "fragment"` for `BrowserOAuthClient`, `authorize()` sends `response_mode` in the PAR body, and `readCallbackParams()` reads `location.hash` in fragment mode. I have the complete picture now, with each leg verified against the live server.

## What's going on: three clients, three different seams

**tangled.org — works because it exercises only what Custos implements.** It's a server-side client (`@atproto/oauth-client-node`), which uses `response_mode=query` and does its token exchange server-to-server. Tonight's log/metrics window shows its textbook flow: 1 PAR → consent → code redirect → 2 token calls (the expected `use_dpop_nonce` 400, then 200). Long-lived sessions = the refresh grant working as intended.

**rpg.actor — Custos silently ignores `response_mode=fragment`.** rpg.actor bundles the official `@atproto/oauth-client-browser`, whose *default* response mode is `fragment`. It asks for the authorization response in the URL fragment (`#code=…`), but our [PARForm](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_par.rs:32) has no `response_mode` field — serde drops it silently — and [`build_code_redirect`](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_templates.rs:66) always emits `?code=…&state=…&iss=…` in the **query string**. Back at `rpg.actor/oauth/callback`, the library reads the (empty) fragment, finds no OAuth params, falls through to "restore existing session", finds none, and their callback script quietly bounces you to `/login`. That's precisely your symptom, and the production counters corroborate it: your three attempts tonight (23:14–23:15Z) produced 3 PARs, 3 wallet-approved consents, 3 code redirects — and **zero** token-endpoint calls. Nothing ever got far enough to fail loudly. (I ruled out the other suspects empirically: CORS is open with all headers exposed, the DPoP-preflight OPTIONS works from rpg.actor's origin, `iss` matches, and their exact PAR request — granular scopes and all — returns 201.)

The subtle spec angle: RFC 8414 says a server that omits `response_modes_supported` implicitly claims support for **both** `query` and `fragment`. We omit it, so the client has no way to know fragment isn't honored.

**pckt.blog — it never does PAR, and only PAR can register a client.** I reproduced its flow: its Laravel backend responds to login with a **direct** `GET /oauth/authorize?client_id=https://pckt.blog/oauth-client-metadata.json&…` — no `request_uri` at all. In Custos, live client-metadata resolution happens *only* inside `/oauth/par`; [`lookup_and_validate_client`](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_authorize.rs:233) at the authorize endpoint is a DB-cache lookup only, so a never-PARed client hits the "client_id is not registered with this server" page. Their metadata document is valid and fetchable (at `/oauth-client-metadata.json` — hyphen, not a path I could guess earlier). Strictly, pckt.blog is the nonconformant party — the [atproto OAuth spec](https://atproto.com/specs/oauth) still says clients "must use PAR" — but bsky.social evidently tolerates direct authorization requests (pckt.blog works there), and the spec explicitly anticipates relaxing PAR to optional.

Optionally advertise `response_modes_supported` in the AS metadata.
2. **Authorize-endpoint client resolution** (fixes the pckt.blog class): on a cache miss for a URL-shaped `client_id`, call the same `resolve_client_metadata` the PAR path uses before rejecting — reference-provider behavior — plus a decision on whether to accept non-PAR authorize requests at all (matching bsky.social's observed leniency) or keep rejecting them, just with an accurate "PAR required" message instead of "not registered".

# Linear Development Workflow

This skill manages the full lifecycle of working on a Linear issue: from picking it up through opening a PR.

## Starting Work on an Issue

When the user indicates they want to work on a Linear issue (e.g., "Let's work on MM-42"):

1. **Parse the issue identifier** from the user's message. The pattern is `MM-` followed by a number.

2. **Fetch the issue details** from Linear using the `get_issue` tool with the parsed identifier. Display a brief summary to the user: title, description (truncated if long), priority, and any existing labels.

3. **Update the issue in Linear:**
   - Set the status to **"In Progress"**
   - Assign it to **"me"** (the authenticated user)

   Use the `save_issue` tool with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Progress"`, and `assignee: "me"`.

4. **Create a git branch from a fresh base** using the issue's suggested branch name:
   - The `get_issue` response includes a `branchName` field — use that as the branch name.
   - **Fetch first, then branch from the remote tip — never from a possibly-stale local HEAD:**
     `git fetch origin main && git checkout -b <branchName> origin/main`
     A stale base silently duplicates work that already merged (hours lost rebuilding an already-shipped backend is the known failure mode).
   - If the branch already exists locally, check it out, then run `git log --oneline <branchName>..origin/main` and surface to the user how far behind the base is.

5. **Verify sibling work is in the base.** If the issue depends on or overlaps sibling issues already marked Done in Linear, confirm their PRs are actually present in the branch base (e.g. `git log --oneline origin/main | grep -i mm-nnn`, or check for the files/routes they added) before concluding any related feature is "missing". **"Linear says Done but the code isn't here" is a hard stop-and-verify signal — it almost always means your base is stale, not that the feature needs building.**

6. **Confirm to the user** what happened: issue assigned, status updated, branch created/checked out (and from which base commit). Then ask what they'd like to tackle first, or summarize the issue so they can dive in.

## Opening a PR (Auto-transition to "In Review")

When the user asks to open a PR, create a pull request, or you detect that a PR is being created for a branch associated with a Linear issue:

1. **Identify the Linear issue** from the current branch name. Linear branch names typically contain the issue identifier (e.g., `malpercio/mm-42-fix-the-thing`). Extract the `MM-XXX` portion.

2. **Create the PR** as the user requests (follow normal PR creation workflow).

3. **After the PR is successfully created**, update the Linear issue:
   - Set the status to **"In Review"**
   - Attach the PR URL as a link on the issue using the `links` field in `save_issue`

   Use `save_issue` with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Review"`, and `links: [{"url": "<pr-url>", "title": "Pull Request"}]`.

4. **Confirm** to the user that the issue has been moved to "In Review" and the PR link has been attached.

- Always fetch the issue first to confirm it exists and get the full `id` (UUID) needed for updates.
- If the issue is already "In Progress" and assigned, skip those updates and just create the branch.
- If branch creation fails (e.g., uncommitted changes), inform the user and suggest next steps rather than silently failing.

Diagnosed live 2026-07-27 with pckt.blog: its Laravel backend never uses PAR — it sends a direct `GET /oauth/authorize?client_id=https://pckt.blog/oauth-client-metadata.json&…`. Their metadata document is valid and fetchable.

Fix: on an authorize-endpoint client-lookup miss for a URL-shaped `client_id`, resolve the metadata document live (reuse `auth::oauth_client_resolution::resolve_client_metadata`) and cache it, matching reference-provider leniency for direct (non-PAR) authorization requests.

86	/// Insert a fresh pending request. `expires_at` is computed as `now + ttl_secs`.
87	pub async fn insert_pending_authorization<'e, E>(
88	    executor: E,
89	    new: &NewPendingOAuthAuthorization<'_>,
90	) -> Result<(), ApiError>
91	where
92	    E: sqlx::Executor<'e, Database = Sqlite>,
93	{
94	    sqlx::query(
95	        "INSERT INTO pending_oauth_authorizations \
96	         (request_id, user_code, client_id, client_name, redirect_uri, code_challenge, \
97	          code_challenge_method, state, response_type, requested_scope, login_hint, origin, ip, \
98	          user_agent, status, created_at, expires_at) \
99	         VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'pending', datetime('now'), \
100	                 datetime('now', ?))",
101	    )
102	    .bind(new.request_id)
103	    .bind(new.user_code)
104	    .bind(new.client_id)
105	    .bind(new.client_name)
106	    .bind(new.redirect_uri)
107	    .bind(new.code_challenge)
108	    .bind(new.code_challenge_method)
109	    .bind(new.state)
110	    .bind(new.response_type)
111	    .bind(new.requested_scope)
112	    .bind(new.login_hint)
113	    .bind(new.origin)
114	    .bind(new.ip)
115	    .bind(new.user_agent)
116	    // A signed modifier string ("+300 seconds" / "-10 seconds"); `{:+}` keeps a negative TTL valid
117	    // (a plain "+{ttl}" would render "+-10 seconds", which SQLite rejects → NULL expiry).
118	    .bind(format!("{:+} seconds", new.ttl_secs))
119	    .execute(executor)
120	    .await
121	    .map_err(|e| {
122	        tracing::error!(error = %e, "DB error inserting pending OAuth authorization");
123	        ApiError::new(
124	            ErrorCode::InternalError,
125	            "failed to create authorization request",
126	        )
127	    })?;
128	    Ok(())
129	}

-- V056: Wallet-confirmed OAuth consent — the pending-authorization primitive.
--
-- A sovereign / migrated account has a NULL password_hash and so cannot pass the
-- password gate on the OAuth consent page (oauth_authorize.rs). This table is the
-- server-side object the consent page creates in place of the password check: a
-- short-lived, single-use request that the wallet approves out-of-band with a
-- device-key-signed envelope (crypto::encode_oauth_consent_envelope), after which the
-- browser completes through the existing authorization-code redirect tail.
--
-- Status is a derived-from-columns state machine (pending → approved → completed, or
-- pending → denied), plus a derived `expired` the read paths compute from `expires_at`
-- rather than persist (no background sweep: lapsed rows are reclaimed opportunistically
-- when the next request is created, matching oauth_par_requests / transfers). Every
-- terminal transition is a guarded single-statement UPDATE, so a replayed approval
-- envelope lands on an already-terminal row and affects zero rows — the request_id
-- binding in the signed envelope plus this single-use row together subsume a separate
-- nonce store.
--
-- `account_did` is deliberately NOT a foreign key to accounts: the row is ephemeral
-- (~5-minute expiry, reclaimed shortly after), the approving DID is already verified

# Changelog fragments

Every pull request that changes a shipped surface must add a short Markdown fragment:

```text
changelog.d/<id>.<type>.md
```

- `<id>` is the Linear issue identifier in lowercase (for example, `mm-358`). If a
  change has no Linear issue, use the pull request number (for example, `271`).
- `<type>` is one of `added`, `changed`, `fixed`, `removed`, or `security`.
- The file contains one concise, user- or operator-facing Markdown statement. Do not
  include a heading or bullet marker; the release script supplies both.
- Use more than one fragment when a change belongs in more than one category.

Example (`changelog.d/mm-358.added.md`):

```markdown
Release notes now collect user-visible changes from pull requests automatically.
```

The CI gate requires a fragment when a pull request changes a deployable surface:

- server or shared runtime source under `crates/*/src/`, plus PDS runtime assets;
- either mobile app's frontend, native runtime source, static assets, or Tauri config;
- the public marketing site;
- the deployed MCP surfaces — the stdio Custos MCP server (`tools/mcp/src/`) and the
  credential-forwarding sidecar (`tools/mcp-sidecar/src/`, plus its image/config), which
  ships as a Railway service and re-exports the stdio server's tool surface;
- workspace runtime dependency manifests, the production image/config, or the NixOS
  runtime module.

Documentation, tests, design files, CI configuration, scripts, developer tooling, and
other repository-internal changes do not trigger the presence requirement. Any fragment
that is present is still checked for a valid name and non-empty content.

The browser test harness (`apps/*/src/lib/harness/`) is developer tooling despite its
path: it is double-gated on `import.meta.env.DEV && VITE_HARNESS` and proven absent from
production builds by `pnpm check:harness-absence`, so the gate skips it explicitly rather
than letting the broad `apps/*/src/` rule claim it.

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

Both CodeRabbit findings were legitimate, and both are fixed, pushed (`9635fc4d`), replied to, and resolved on [PR #478](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/478):

1. **Unthrottled outbound fetches for failing `client_id`s (Major, security)** — real: both `/oauth/par` and the new authorize branch are unauthenticated, and a replayed failing client_id would trigger a fresh outbound fetch each time (bounded only by the per-IP limiter and 5s timeout). Fix: [oauth_client_resolution.rs](crates/pds/src/auth/oauth_client_resolution.rs) now keeps a bounded, process-local 60-second negative cache of failed resolutions — the retry short-circuits with a distinct `RecentlyFailed` error, oldest entries are evicted at 1024 so rotating client_ids can't grow it. This hardens the pre-existing PAR path too, not just the new authorize branch.

2. **`ResponseMode` homed in a routes module (Major, maintainability)** — fair per the repo's "shared logic belongs in `auth/`" rule, since `oauth_par` had started importing `oauth_templates`. Fix: moved to a new [auth/oauth_response_mode.rs](crates/pds/src/auth/oauth_response_mode.rs) (Functional Core, with the parse/separator unit tests moved along); all four consumers now import it from `auth/` and no route-to-route import remains.

# IncludeScope Permission Handling

## inheritAud with No aud Parameter

When an RPC permission has `inheritAud: true` but the include scope lacks an `aud` parameter, the code **does not apply inheritance**. The relevant logic states:

> "rpc" permissions can "inherit" their audience from "aud" param defined in the "include:<nsid>?aud=<audience>" scope the permission set was loaded from.

The condition requires `this.aud !== undefined`, so if the include scope provides no audience, the permission retains its original definition without modification. No error is thrown; the permission is simply processed as-is.

## RPC Permission Rendering

RPC permissions are converted to scope strings through the `buildPermissions()` generator. Each permission yielded calls `p.toString()`, where the RpcPermission class implements formatting. The code treats RPC permissions as resource-based entities subject to authority validation—they must fall under the lexicon's namespace authority to be included.

# RPC Permission `aud` Parameter Analysis

**Required Status:** The `aud` parameter is **required** for RPC permissions.

**Parsing/Validation Logic:** 
The parser configuration specifies `"multiple: false, required: true, validate: isAudParam"`. This means an RPC permission cannot be created without an `aud` value—if it's absent, parsing will fail and return `null`.

**Matching Behavior:**
When a permission has `aud === '*'`, the matching logic allows any audience: `"(aud === '*' || aud === options.aud)"`. However, there's a critical constraint: the code explicitly forbids the combination `"rpc:*?aud=*"` by returning `null` during parsing, preventing a permission that wildcard-matches both the LXM (lexicon method) and audience simultaneously.

input.title: Permission-set expansion: skip unconvertible entries (reference parity) — include:app.bsky.authCreatePosts fails the whole set on an inheritAud rpc entry
input.description:
Follow-up to MM-489, diagnosed live 2026-07-28 with pckt.blog after the authorize-endpoint client resolution shipped: the flow now reaches consent-scope expansion and dies there with `invalid_scope: "app.bsky.authCreatePosts" contains an invalid permission entry`, which pckt.blog surfaces as "Something went wrong during login."

Root cause: Bluesky's published `app.bsky.authCreatePosts` permission set contains an rpc entry `{lxm: [app.bsky.video.*], resource: "rpc", inheritAud: true}` with no `aud`. pckt's `include:app.bsky.authCreatePosts` token carries no `?aud=`, so the entry renders as an `rpc:` token without `aud` — invalid in the scope grammar — and Custos's `resolve_permission_set` fails the **whole set** closed.

The reference (`@atproto/oauth-scopes` `IncludeScope.buildPermissions`) instead **silently skips** any entry that cannot be converted (`if (!syntax) continue; if (!resourcePermission) continue`) — so bsky.social expands the same include to just the repo-create grant and pckt.blog works there. The reference also drops rpc entries carrying an explicit non-`*` `aud` inside a set.

Fix: match reference semantics in `auth/permission_sets.rs::resolve_permission_set` — skip (with a debug log) entries that fail to render/normalize, and skip rpc entries with a defined non-`*` aud; keep hard failures for fetch/shape-level problems (unresolvable NSID, no defs, not a permission-set, malformed JSON). Skipping only ever narrows the grant, and both the GET display expansion and the POST authoritative expansion apply the same rule, so what the user sees stays what is granted.

This one's not us anymore — **Custos is now doing everything right, and the remaining failure is a ~30-second login-state TTL inside pckt.blog itself.** Here's the proof chain:

**Your real attempts completed fully on our side.** Both tries (wallet approvals logged at 01:41:26 and 01:42:01) rendered the consent page — so the MM-490 scope-expansion fix is confirmed working live — issued a code, and 303'd it back to pckt's callback. - authorize error redirects — error code + client_id

- **Every token/revocation rejection** (`OAuthTokenError::into_response`): error code + description — makes `invalid_grant` vs `use_dpop_nonce` vs missing-parameter distinguishable from `railway logs` in one look
- **Every authorization error redirect** (`error_redirect`): error + description — these deliver the error to the *client*, so the operator otherwise sees only a bare 3xx
- **Each completed authorization-code exchange**: `client_id` + DID, the counterpart of `oauth_consent`'s approve log

Mechanical facts only — codes, fixed descriptions, client ids, DIDs; never token material.
